summary:
Baja California is among the Mexican states that have legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition. The state congress created the procedure through a 2022 reform to the Civil Code, initially limited to adults. In June 2023 the Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation invalidated the 18-years requirement, holding that the law failed to recognise the rights of transgender children and adolescents, and the state congress responded with a further reform in 2024 establishing a procedure for individuals under 18 and extending legal gender recognition to non-binary people.

No criminalisation of trans presence applies. The national framework, as Human Rights Watch set out on 31 March 2025, leaves legal gender recognition to the states and records a patchwork of procedures whose implementation differs sharply; where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation. Baja California sits on the reformed side of that patchwork, but the gap between statute and practice documented across Mexico applies here as elsewhere: Caroline Beer's analysis for LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly.

Lethal violence against women in the state is under-classified. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 March 2025 that under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila 1,179 women have been killed in Baja California while only 110 cases were typified as feminicide. The same reporting places female economic participation in the state at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 states.

Extradition machinery has been used in feminicide cases. Zeta Tijuana reported on 8 July 2023 that Brayan Rivera was presented on 6 July 2023 before US Judge Karen L. Stevenson in provisional detention for extradition, accused by Mexico of the feminicide of Ángela Carolina Acosta, killed on 24 January 2022 in room 404 of Hotel Cascadas beside Bar Hong Kong in Tijuana's tolerance zone. A US federal court determined probable cause on 29 June 2023; he was arrested at his parents' Downey, California home, where officers found the Hotel Cascadas rent receipt and rope and gloves. At a 7 July 2023 press conference the Baja California attorney general called the 30-year-old a serial perpetrator, said extradition could take from 15 days to two years, and that nearly a decade of open case files were being reviewed; the investigation had linked him to at least three feminicides: Ángela (January 2022), Elizabeth (14 February), and Karen, 28 (30 August 2021, Motel Hacienda Soler).

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009.
tangentialFactors:
Impunity for lethal violence is the national backdrop. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that Mexico City criminalised transfemicide on 18 July 2024 under the Paola Buenrostro law, with sentences of up to 70 years, in one of Latin America's deadliest settings for trans people; nationally, over 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022. Baja California has not enacted an equivalent transfemicide statute.

Where a Mexican state has no recognition procedure, the consequences are documented. Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024 on Tabasco found that the absence of a procedure exposes trans people to institutional mistreatment: the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling legal names. Baja California's procedure removes that particular exposure but does not by itself guarantee respectful treatment in healthcare or police settings.

Violence against trans people nationally intensified over the year to mid-2024, with at least three transgender people killed in the opening weeks of 2024 and attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rising over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition in Baja California use the administrative procedure created by the 2022 Civil Code reform and expanded by the 2024 reform, which now covers individuals under 18 and recognises non-binary people. The Supreme Court's June 2023 ruling striking down the adults-only requirement is the authority under which minors may apply.

Under-classification of feminicide is a live concern for residents. Zeta Tijuana's 8 March 2025 reporting shows 1,179 women killed in the state under Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila against 110 cases typified as feminicide, and places female economic participation at roughly 46-47%, 14th of 32 states.

The state attorney general's office has pursued long-running feminicide investigations, including the Rivera case in which nearly a decade of open files were reviewed and at least three killings were linked to one suspect.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Baja California's recognition procedure is applied without delay or obstruction in practice is not sourced here; the Human Rights Watch tracker records the procedure's existence and the Supreme Court rulings driving expansion, but state-level implementation quality for Baja California specifically remains unresolved.

Whether Baja California's criminal code carries hate-motivation provisions comparable to or absent from Tabasco's is not stated in the inventory and is unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses restroom or facilities access, healthcare access for trans residents, or police treatment of trans people in Baja California specifically; these remain not sourced.
